blocks.body:
With a 6-litre jug and a 10-litre jug and an unlimited tap, which amounts of water can you measure? Every amount you can produce has the form $6x + 10y$ for some integers $x$ and $y$ (negative values mean pouring out), so the question is which integers can be written that way. All of them are even, so $3$ is impossible. But $2 = 6 \cdot 2 + 10 \cdot (-1)$ is possible, and then every even number is.

The pattern is general. The integer combinations $ax + by$ are exactly the multiples of $\gcd(a,b)$, and the Euclidean algorithm, run backwards, tells you how to find the coefficients. This lesson proves that and uses it to solve every equation $ax + by = c$ in integers.

blocks.title: Which numbers are combinations?
blocks.body:
Fix $a = 6$, $b = 10$, and list some values of $6x + 10y$: with $(x, y) = (1, 0), (0, 1), (2, -1), (-3, 2), (5, -3)$ we get $6, 10, 2, 2, 0$. Every value is divisible by $\gcd(6,10) = 2$, since $2$ divides both $6$ and $10$. The surprise is the reverse direction: $2$ itself shows up, and then $2k = 6(2k) + 10(-k)$ for every $k$.

Why should the gcd always be reachable? Think of the Euclidean algorithm. Each remainder is the previous number minus a multiple of the one before it, so each remainder is an integer combination of the two numbers you started with. The last non-zero remainder is the gcd, so the gcd is an integer combination of $a$ and $b$. The theorem below makes this precise with a short argument, and the next section turns the idea into an algorithm.

blocks.title: Bézout's identity
blocks.body:
Let $a$ and $b$ be integers, not both zero. Then there are integers $x$ and $y$ with
$$ax + by = \gcd(a,b).$$
Moreover, the set $\{ax + by : x, y \in \mathbb Z\}$ is exactly the set of multiples of $\gcd(a,b)$.

blocks.title: Proof of Bézout's identity
blocks.body:
Let $S = \{ax + by : x, y \in \mathbb Z\}$. It contains the positive number $a^2 + b^2$, so it has a smallest positive element; call it $d = ax_0 + by_0$.

We show $d \mid a$. Divide with remainder: $a = qd + r$ with $0 \le r < d$. Then
$$r = a - q(ax_0 + by_0) = a(1 - qx_0) + b(-qy_0),$$
so $r$ is also in $S$. Since $0 \le r < d$ and $d$ is the smallest positive element of $S$, we must have $r = 0$. So $d \mid a$, and in the same way $d \mid b$. Hence $d$ is a common divisor, and $d \le g$ where $g = \gcd(a,b)$.

On the other hand $g$ divides $a$ and $b$, so it divides $ax_0 + by_0 = d$, which gives $g \le d$. Therefore $d = g$, proving the first claim.

For the second claim: every element of $S$ is divisible by $g$ (as $g \mid a$ and $g \mid b$), and every multiple $kg = a(kx_0) + b(ky_0)$ lies in $S$.

blocks.title: The extended Euclidean algorithm
blocks.body:
The proof above shows the coefficients exist but does not find them. To find them, run the Euclidean algorithm and keep track of how each remainder is built from $a$ and $b$. For $a = 1071$ and $b = 462$ the algorithm read $1071 = 2\cdot 462 + 147$, $462 = 3 \cdot 147 + 21$, $147 = 7 \cdot 21$. Solve each line for its remainder and substitute upwards:
$$\begin{aligned} 21 &= 462 - 3 \cdot 147 \\ &= 462 - 3\,(1071 - 2 \cdot 462) \\ &= 7 \cdot 462 - 3 \cdot 1071. \end{aligned}$$
So $1071 \cdot (-3) + 462 \cdot 7 = 21$.

For hand or computer work it is tidier to go forwards with a table. Keep rows $(r, x, y)$ with $r = ax + by$. Start with $(a, 1, 0)$ and $(b, 0, 1)$. If the last two rows are $R_{i-1}$ and $R_i$ and $q$ is the quotient of $r_{i-1}$ by $r_i$, the next row is $R_{i-1} - q R_i$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|r|r} q & r & x & y \\ \hline & 1071 & 1 & 0 \\ & 462 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 147 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 21 & -3 & 7 \\ 7 & 0 & 22 & -51 \end{array}$$
The row with the last non-zero remainder gives the Bézout coefficients. The final row is a nice bonus: $1071 \cdot 22 - 462 \cdot 51 = 0$, and $22 = 462/21$, $51 = 1071/21$. It hands you the step between solutions, which is the subject of the theorem on linear Diophantine equations below.

blocks.title: Euclid's lemma (general form)
blocks.body: If $m \mid kn$ and $\gcd(m, k) = 1$, then $m \mid n$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: By Bézout there are integers $u, v$ with $mu + kv = 1$. Multiply by $n$: $n = m(nu) + (kn)v$. Both terms on the right are divisible by $m$, the second because $m \mid kn$. So $m \mid n$.

blocks.title: Linear Diophantine equations in two variables
blocks.body:
Let $a, b$ be non-zero integers, $g = \gcd(a,b)$ and $c$ an integer. The equation
$$ax + by = c$$
has an integer solution if and only if $g \mid c$. If $(x_0, y_0)$ is one solution, then all integer solutions are
$$x = x_0 + \frac{b}{g}\,t, \qquad y = y_0 - \frac{a}{g}\,t, \qquad t \in \mathbb Z.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Solvability is the second half of Bézout's identity: the values of $ax + by$ are exactly the multiples of $g$.

Plugging in shows each pair in the family is a solution, since $a \cdot \frac{b}{g}t - b\cdot\frac{a}{g}t = 0$. Conversely let $(x, y)$ be any solution. Subtracting $ax_0 + by_0 = c$ gives $a(x - x_0) = -b(y - y_0)$, and dividing by $g$,
$$\frac{a}{g}(x - x_0) = -\frac{b}{g}(y - y_0).$$
The numbers $a/g$ and $b/g$ are coprime: from $ax_0' + by_0' = g$ (Bézout) we get $\frac{a}{g}x_0' + \frac{b}{g}y_0' = 1$, and any common divisor of $a/g$ and $b/g$ divides $1$. Now $b/g$ divides $\frac{a}{g}(x - x_0)$ and is coprime to $a/g$, so by Euclid's lemma $\frac{b}{g} \mid x - x_0$. Write $x - x_0 = \frac{b}{g}t$. Substituting back gives $\frac{a}{g}\cdot\frac{b}{g}t = -\frac{b}{g}(y - y_0)$, and dividing by $\frac{b}{g} \neq 0$ gives $y - y_0 = -\frac{a}{g}t$.

blocks.title: Running the algorithm backwards
blocks.solution:
Euclidean algorithm:
$$\begin{aligned} 240 &= 5 \cdot 46 + 10 \\ 46 &= 4 \cdot 10 + 6 \\ 10 &= 1 \cdot 6 + 4 \\ 6 &= 1 \cdot 4 + 2 \\ 4 &= 2 \cdot 2 + 0 \end{aligned}$$
so the gcd is $2$. Back-substitute:
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= 6 - 4 = 6 - (10 - 6) = 2 \cdot 6 - 10 \\ &= 2(46 - 4 \cdot 10) - 10 = 2 \cdot 46 - 9 \cdot 10 \\ &= 2 \cdot 46 - 9(240 - 5 \cdot 46) = 47 \cdot 46 - 9 \cdot 240. \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -9$, $y = 47$. Check: $47 \cdot 46 = 2162$ and $9 \cdot 240 = 2160$.

blocks.title: Coprime divisors multiply
blocks.body: Show that if $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, $a \mid c$ and $b \mid c$, then $ab \mid c$.
blocks.solution:
Choose $x, y$ with $ax + by = 1$ and multiply by $c$: $c = acx + bcy$. Since $b \mid c$, the product $ab$ divides $ac$; since $a \mid c$, it divides $bc$. So $ab$ divides both terms, hence divides $c$.

Without the coprimality the claim fails: $4 \mid 12$ and $6 \mid 12$ but $24 \nmid 12$.

blocks.title: A word problem
blocks.body: Pens cost 15 units and notebooks 21 units. Someone spent exactly 261 units and bought at least one of each. What could they have bought?
blocks.solution:
We need positive integers with $15x + 21y = 261$. Here $\gcd(15, 21) = 3$ and $3 \mid 261$, so solutions exist; divide by $3$ to get $5x + 7y = 87$.

A Bézout relation for $5$ and $7$ is $5 \cdot 3 + 7 \cdot (-2) = 1$. Multiplying by $87$ gives the particular solution $(x_0, y_0) = (261, -174)$, and by the theorem every solution is
$$x = 261 + 7t, \qquad y = -174 - 5t.$$
Positivity needs $261 + 7t > 0$, i.e. $t \ge -37$, and $-174 - 5t > 0$, i.e. $t \le -35$. So $t \in \{-37, -36, -35\}$, giving
$$(x, y) = (2, 11),\ (9, 6),\ (16, 1).$$
Check one: $15 \cdot 9 + 21 \cdot 6 = 135 + 126 = 261$. Note how the step from one answer to the next is $(7, -5) = (21/3, -15/3)$.

blocks.title: The largest amount you cannot pay
blocks.body: Let $a, b$ be coprime positive integers. Call $n$ representable if $n = ax + by$ with $x, y \ge 0$. Show that $ab - a - b$ is not representable, but every integer larger than it is.
blocks.solution:
Fix an integer $n$. All integer solutions of $ax + by = n$ are $x = x_0 + bt$, $y = y_0 - at$. Exactly one of them has $0 \le x \le b - 1$ (choose $t$ so that $x_0 + bt$ is the remainder of $x_0$ on division by $b$). Call this the standard solution $(x^*, y^*)$.

Among all solutions with $x \ge 0$, the standard one has the largest $y$, because increasing $t$ increases $x$ and decreases $y$, and decreasing $t$ below the standard value makes $x$ negative. So $n$ is representable exactly when $y^* \ge 0$.

For $n = ab - a - b = a(b - 1) + b(-1)$, the standard solution is $x^* = b - 1$, $y^* = -1 < 0$. So $ab - a - b$ is not representable.

If $n > ab - a - b$, then $by^* = n - ax^* \ge n - a(b-1) > ab - a - b - ab + a = -b$. So $y^* > -1$, that is $y^* \ge 0$, and $n$ is representable.

For example with $a = 5$, $b = 7$ the largest non-representable number is $35 - 12 = 23$. This is the two-coin case of the Frobenius coin problem.

blocks.body:
- The Bézout coefficients are not unique: $6 \cdot 2 + 10 \cdot (-1) = 2$ and $6 \cdot (-3) + 10 \cdot 2 = 2$. They differ by multiples of $(b/g, -a/g)$.
- If $ax + by = d$ you may only conclude $\gcd(a,b) \mid d$, not $d = \gcd(a,b)$: $6 \cdot 1 + 10 \cdot 1 = 16$. The exception is $d = 1$, which does force $\gcd(a, b) = 1$.
- The general solution steps by $b/g$ and $a/g$, not by $b$ and $a$. Using $b$ and $a$ misses solutions whenever $g > 1$.
- Bézout gives integer coefficients, usually one negative. Whether non-negative coefficients exist is a different question (the last example).

The most important use comes next: a relation $ax + ny = 1$ says exactly that $ax \equiv 1 \pmod n$, so Bézout computes [[mod-inverse|modular inverses]], and through them the [[crt]]. Euclid's lemma for primes, the key to unique factorisation in [[fta]], is the special case $m = p$ of the lemma above.

In the language of algebra, the set $S$ in the proof is the ideal generated by $a$ and $b$, and the theorem says it is generated by the single number $\gcd(a,b)$. Rings in which every ideal is generated by one element are called principal ideal domains; see [[ideals]]. The [[gaussian-integers]] have their own division with remainder and hence their own Bézout identity. Equations with more variables or higher degree are taken up in [[diophantine]].

1. Find integers $x, y$ with $101x + 37y = 1$.
2. Find all integer solutions of $14x - 35y = 21$.
3. Prove that $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ if and only if there are integers $x, y$ with $ax + by = 1$.
4. With a 9-litre and a 15-litre jug, can you measure exactly 4 litres? Exactly 6 litres?
